grain sales proceeds rather than on the financial balance in the fund. I leave that for the minister's consideration.
The issue of the plan being based on net income rather than gross income was thoroughly fought the first time, the legislation came before us in 1971. One of the main arguments we put up at that time was that it should be based on net income and not gross income, and there should be provision for accounting and for increasing costs of production-some form of escalation to provide for increasing costs of production.
I want to say here that the minister has come around some distance, and this is not usual for him when dealing with this parliament or previous parliaments. He came around to the view that the plan would be better if it were based on net income rather than gross income, and that the matter of costs of production has to be brought in. It is almost a 180 degree turn. As I recall the speeches made on the government side in 1971, we were told that it was impossible and could not be done, etc. I wish the minister had come all the way though, because in arriving at net cash flow, when you look at the eligible expenses that are considered as deductions from the gross cash income, there are some legitimate cash expenses that are excluded from the legislation.
The bill includes only cash expenses incurred in the production and sale of grain as eligible expenses. It excludes depreciation on farm machinery, it excludes interest on equity, and it excludes the labour and management of the producer. I am particularly unhappy to see that interest on indebtedness is excluded because that is a cash expenditure that grain producers have every year. In particular, interest on indebtedness for buildings and farm machinery is a large expenditure for grain producers in western Canada.
I think the minister errs in at least not allowing the interest on indebtedness for things like buildings and farm machinery to be included. The price of farm machinery has reached heights that were not imagined five or ten years ago, and most farm machinery purchases are financed at interest rates of 10 per cent or 15 per cent. The farmer has to make cash payments on that machinery every year, and of course the payments include interest on the loans.
I can see that there might be some argument against allowing interest on land indebtedness since land usually appreciates. There may be temporary drops in land values, but I do not see any significant permanent drop in the near future. An argument could be made that interest on payments for land should be excluded, but I think there is no justification for excluding interest payments on buildings and machinery, both of which are depreciating assets.
The minister has excluded depreciation from the bill. Since the facilities I have mentioned on grain farms are not going to appreciate in the way that land will, surely depreciation on buildings and machinery should be allowed as an expense. I appreciate it is not a cash expense. That would be a departure from one of the main features of the bill which reflects cash income and cash expenses, but I hope the minister will look at it again.
I am happy to see that income received under the crop insurance program will be calculated as part of the total

April 30, 1975
Western Grain Stabilization
gross income and that this will allow farmers to contribute more to the fund. I submit there are too many exclusions, however, and the bill should be amended to allow the inclusion of interest on at least farm buildings and machinery, and to allow the depreciation on buildings and machinery.
There are many implications in the aggregate calculations of payouts over the entire Wheat Board region. Because the plan operates on an aggregate basis, all regions and all grains are lumped together in the calculation of aggregate payouts. This offers little or no protection on a regional or on a commodity basis.
For example, Madam Speaker, if rapeseed producers experience a badly depressed market but all other grains do very well, there is no payout for rapeseed producers from the plan if the aggreagate proceeds from all the other grains remain at or above the five year average level. Similarly, an individual producer's share of the aggregate payout when a stabilization payment is made is determined in proportion to his share of contribution through the levies in that year and the immediately preceding two years. In other words, a producer who has had good sales, and therefore has made a relatively substantial contribution to the fund, will receive a proportionately higher payout, whereas a producer who has done less well in sales will receive proportionately less. It seems to me that as the bill stands now it rewards good fortune and penalizes misfortune. The one who needs the most gets the least, and I think that is a fundamental weakness in the legislation.
The minister mentioned on a previous occasion the possibility of paying out on a local or regional basis rather than on the aggregate of the entire grains income over the entire Wheat Board area. Having listened to the minister and read his speech, I am under the impression he will be willing to look at these things until he has had time to become experienced in the administration of the legislation and devise ways, administratively and technically, of paying out on a regional or local basis. I do not think that difficulty is insurmountable. It can be done.
I am thinking of a particular situation. Say that in a large area of northeastern Saskatchewan, northwestern Alberta, or in the Peace River country, farmers raise abundant, but low grade crops in one year. Let us say the demand for high grades of grain is strong, that the demand on domestic and export markets is strong for Nos. 1, 2 and 3 wheat, for example. What will happen? The farmers in a large area where low grades of grain are grown will have low sales; but there will be no payout for them, because if the aggregate of all sales is at or about the five-year average, it means the people in the large area who have raised poor or low grade crops will not get any payout. Again, the ones who need help most will get least. In the circumstances I mentioned they may not get anything at all. I suggest that the minister, his officials, the committee, and other organizations must put their heads together and devise ways to change the legislation so that payouts on a regional or local basis can be made.
The stabilization effect of the plan is reduced by a number of other factors. In a period of decline the five-year average would become progressively lower; net

income would show a progressive decline and producers would continue to contribute the levy. Payouts would occur during periods of relatively high but falling commodity prices, but no payouts would occur during periods of relatively low but rising prices. I submit that the cost of the plan to the federal government is overstated and the stabilization effect reduced, because a portion of federal contributions, around 15 per cent, would be recovered through taxation when a payment is made. What they give with one hand, they take back with the other. At least they take back a good chunk.
Because the stabilized margin, the net cash flow, as the minister puts it, is not indexed to inflation, net income would decline in terms of real dollars at a rate approximately equal to the rate of inflation with no support payments being made.
Stabilization payments themselves are not included as proceeds in calculating the five-year average. This I do not understand. The levy is based on the financial position of the stabilization fund, and not on ability to pay. The levy could actually increase in a bad year. Further, the support level drops to 90 per cent of the five-year average after the fund has been in a deficit position for three years. Surely that is exactly when support should increase. Obviously grain farmers will be in difficulty at that point in time.
The assumption underlying the plan is the continued operation of a free market, which makes one laugh, and the need to protect producers from its fluctuations. That is understandable. Production surpluses and deficits will continue to exist. The government is to play no active role in determining the allocation of productive resources.
I return to what I said at the beginning of my speech. My party thinks there is a simpler and better way of doing this. I admit, without hesitation or sorrow, that our plan would require higher expenditures from the federal treasury than the present plan. I think it is only fair that there should be some contribution by farmers in other ways, such as through crop insurance, and so on. In other words they should pay some kind of premium.
The most effective way of stabilizing income, it seems to me, is to establish a system of guaranteed prices for all grains. These prices should be related to costs of production. As well, an escalating factor should be included to take care of annual increases in production costs. Such guaranteed prices would assure farmers of a certain level of income. There will be years, obviously, when prices will be down and the federal treasury may need to inject up to several hundred millions of dollars into the scheme in order to maintain guaranteed prices for producers. No doubt from time to time commodities other than grain will be affected.
If the guaranteed price imposes hardship on certain segments of the public, on consumers, the government should look at the other side of the coin and come in with a form of consumer subsidy. We are doing this with two-price wheat and there is no reason why this cannot be extended to cover all grains. Frankly I think it should cover all agricultural production. That, surely, would be administratively easier than what is contemplated under this bill. Surely such a scheme would do a better job in providing for farm income security.
April 30, 1975

I know the idea is somewhat socialistic, but this has been done by countries with so-called free enterprise governments, or governments operating under variations of that principle. Surely that would be an easier and better way. Under such a system we could guarantee the farmer a price for his grain, a price that would return to him his full costs of production and a decent living. That guarantee would come from all the people of Canada. That, I think, would be a system far more effective than any system contemplated by this legislation, which is so complicated, so full of legal gobbledygook. I suspect that we shall need to hire quite a few more public servants to administer this legislation. We shall need more than we needed to administer PFAA and other programs like it. I am afraid this will become an administrative nightmare, largely because of the way the minister has chosen to implement the grain stabilization plan.
I repeat, that we think it essential for this bill to receive the most thorough scrutiny by the committee. The committee must hold hearings in two or three dozen places at least in the Wheat Board area. It must receive briefs and submissions from grain producers and organizations representing them. They should be allowed to ask their questions, although I doubt if we will be able to answer them all, because it is still difficult to understand how this bill is to apply. Further, I hope the minister and his officials will use the simplest English possible when giving answers. I am not hopeful on that score, but I hope that his officials will work on this idea.

I hope the minister will be agreeable to improving it and changing it, or more agreeable to doing this than he was on the previous occasion. I hope more attention will be paid to the views of farm organizations who represent grain producers in western Canada. Again, I hope that more attention will be paid than was paid on the prior occasion, Madam Speaker.
On a point of order, Madam Speaker, may I inquire if we are to be told what the business will be tomorrow and on Friday?
